# 10-palus: sources

Back-test entry `10-palus.yaml`: Palus Finance, more yield on a startup's idle cash (YC Winter 2026). Written 2026-10-22 from public material only. Quotes are verbatim. **[author]** marks a choice the public material does not make, kept as small as it could be.

Sources, with the short names used below:
- **HN**: Launch HN, 2026-03-06, https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=47278980 (the founders' post and 89 comments). A comment is cited as HN/NNN, meaning https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=NNN.
- **YCL**: Launch YC post, https://www.ycombinator.com/launches/PfC-palus-finance-better-yields-on-idle-cash-for-startups-and-smbs
- **YCC**: YC company page, https://www.ycombinator.com/companies/palus-finance
- **SITE**: https://palus.finance and https://www.palus.finance/treasury (read 2026-10-22)

Status today: same customer, a wider offer. The YC page says "Palus is your startup's financial advisor". The homepage now says "The world's most advanced fractional CFO firm" (SITE). The treasury product is still on /treasury.

## The eight founder-emulation items

**1. Who (actor, segment, roles).** The founder was his own customer:
- "we realized we needed the product for our own startup’s cash reserves, and other startups in the batch started telling us they wanted this too" (HN).
- The co-founder named who it is for: "this product is for startups and SMBs that don't have the time or resources to host a fractional CFO or a full-time finance team" (HN/47283812).
- A sceptic named the two people whose time it costs: "the founder, or an ops person's time" (HN/47297953).
- *Roles.* Keel's B2B shape needs one role that lives the problem and another that decides to buy. At a funded startup the person who moves the cash every month is the one who runs finance day to day (a finance or ops lead, or a fractional CFO). The person who signs where the reserve sits is the founder-CEO. The founders aim their product and copy at founders: "We optimized our UX for founders" (HN/47290652). So `finance_lead` is the practitioner (12 people, Parts 1 and 2) and `founder` is the decision-maker (8 people, Part 3). The same company pays.
- **[author]** The split is mine. At the smallest startups the two roles are one person. That is why one practitioner (Grace Mbeki) passes the job to a fractional CFO, and why the commercial vector is read from founders.
- *Segment*: "Startups and SMBs" banking with "Brex, Mercury, etc." (HN). **[author]** I narrowed it to US venture-backed startups within two years of a raise, to match the occasion the founder describes.

**2. What (the job).** The job is to earn more on the cash without risking it and without switching banks:
- "earn higher yields with a high-yield bond portfolio" (HN).
- "a way to earn more yield on fundraise proceeds without switching banks" (YCC, as summarised from the page).
- Context job **[author]**, worded from these: "keep the money from a raise safe and earning until the company spends it".

**3. When / where (circumstance, occasion, window).**
- "The typical startup cashflow pattern is a large infusion from a raise covering 18–24 months of burn, drawn down gradually" (HN).
- "you’re giving up yield to get same-day liquidity on cash you won’t touch for six months or more" (HN).
- The repeated moment is the monthly transfer: "easy to set up rules like ("if my bank balance falls below $X then transfer $Y from treasury")" (HN/47280293).
- **[author]** The occasion "cash decision", the window {3, MONTHS}, Frequency 2 to 3 months out of 3, and Prevalence "Most" (p_60_80) are mine. They follow from "drawn down gradually" (a monthly move), and they match 05-paidly's three-month window.

**4. Which people (comparable group).**
- "Say you (like many startups) use Mercury Treasury, Rho Treasury, Brex Treasury, etc." (HN/47280293).
- "founders who've thought about idle cash management" (HN).
- **[author]** The Importance rivals come from what the thread itself raises:
  - runway: "an extra month or two of runway", HN/47282750
  - safety above the insured limit: the SVB-style worry in HN/47279304 and HN/47279349
  - getting cash back fast: "1-2 business days", HN
  - moving money without mistakes: "no manual reconciliation between accounts", HN/47283812

**5. Who pays.**
- The company pays a fee on its own balance: "We will charge a flat 0.25% annual fee on AUM" (HN).
- The founder decides. The pitch is to the founder's time: "It's a one-time setup that takes five minutes. We optimized our UX for founders" (HN/47290652).
- Buyer and payer:
  - **[author]** The founder's tested item is "Nobody else", which fits the five-minute pitch.
  - "The board" is the one other role on the founder's list. The thread itself puts it there: "I am not sure I would suggest my portfolio companies to risk their treasuries" (HN/47279377). SITE also says the design follows "NVCA startup treasury guidelines".
- Purchase friction:
  - "Diligence on a new provider" comes from "it definitely takes weeks to diligence your company and the offering" (HN/47401784).
  - "A tax adviser's sign-off" comes from "they should talk to their tax advisor" (HN/47282781).
  - "Board approval of the cash policy" **[author]**.

**6. Mechanism.**
- "we built Palus to connect to your existing bank account via Plaid" (HN).
- "Our bond portfolio holds short-duration floating-rate" government-backed mortgage-backed securities, "managed by Regan Capital, which runs MBSF" (HN).
- "Liquidity is typically available in 1-2 business days" (HN).
- "All assets are held with an SEC-licensed custodian" (HN).
- "two buttons and a giant number that goes up" (HN).
- Compatibility conditions, Adoption friction efforts and the Commitment step:
  - The tested condition, "They could wait two days for their cash", is the founder's own claim: "most startups can afford to take on a bit more liquidity risk on their long-term cash (on the order of a couple of days)" (HN/47282907).
  - The commitment step comes from "I'd encourage you to start small, try us out, and grow your position over time" (HN/47280532).
  - The tested effort, "Move the long-term reserve out of the bank's treasury", **[author]**, worded from "The problem is the treasury product bundled with them, not the bank" (HN).

**7. Price.**
- "We will charge a flat 0.25% annual fee on AUM, compared to the 0.15–0.60%, depending on balance, charged by other treasury providers" (HN).
- "Rho charges a variable rate that peaks at 0.6% for any deposit of $2M or less" (HN/47280707).
- Yields: "we target 4.5–5% returns vs. roughly 3.5% from most money market funds" (HN). SITE now says "targeted SOFR + 1% spread".
- **[author]** Keel's price is a money range over a period, and its ladder stops below $10,000. So I state the fee per month on the reserve the founder's own example uses, $4M to $6M: 0.25% of that is $10,000 to $15,000 a year, so $800 to $1,200 a month.
- **[author]** The cost estimate, $4,000 to $6,000 a month, is the yield given up. The founder says "on $5M, it's an extra $50k-75k per year" (HN/47280107), which is about $4,200 to $6,250 a month, rounded to the range. It counts yield given up, which the registry's meaning allows ("foregone alternatives"). It does not count the 0.15% to 0.60% fee the bank's product already takes.
- **[author]** The hourly rate, $75, is mine: a startup finance lead's salary of about $150k a year, over a working year.
- Ability to pay is derived by code: 13% to 30%, small_share.

**8. Occasions (real accounts).**
- No named customer quote is public. HN is the record: batchmates "started telling us they wanted this too" (HN), one sign-up, "I’ve wanted this produce for years. Signed up." (HN/47283895), and many sceptics. Each respondent below is traced to one of them.

## Respondents

Practitioners (primary link, `finance_lead`):
- Dana Whitfield: HN/47279411 ("we wouldn't want to switch even for a higher yield… the operational burden is more important to us than yield", "about 3.2%"). The $300k transfer is **[author]**.
- Marcus Oyelaran: HN/47279219 (self-directed brokerage, "more paperwork and back and forth", then "click that button now!"). The $3M and August are **[author]**.
- Lena Hofstra: HN/47279349 ("nowhere near juicy enough for me to literally bet the company on") and HN/47279304 (bank-run worry). The Treasuries-only policy and the two banks are **[author]**, after the 2023 bank failures the thread refers to.
- Tomás Reyes: HN/47283895 ("I’ve wanted this produce for years"), with the launch post's "large infusion from a raise". Cash sitting in plain checking is **[author]**.
- Aisha Karimi: HN/47279292 ("business savings accounts not much below this (2.85%) while keeping things safe (FDIC insured)").
- Ben Okafor: HN/47280707 (the fee "peaks at 0.6% for any deposit of $2M or less"). The $1.5M is **[author]**.
- Rachel Lindqvist: HN/47282512 and HN/47283590 (PHC and QSBS: "a bunch of startups are raising $20m on $0 revenue … interest … can easily be the only income").
- Hiro Tanabe (gate No): HN/47279242 ("Startups otherwise are lean and won't hold enough cash to get a meaningful return").
- Grace Mbeki: HN/47283265 ("they might be better suited to deal with a fractional CFO service"). The Slack approval is **[author]**; the YC page (YCC) says the firm is reachable around the clock on Slack (paraphrased).
- Owen Castellano (chip): author's invention, filling a gap: no commenter refuses to say. A chipped story is needed so the reading counts one GUESSED person. It loosely echoes HN/47279377 (an investor steering portfolio companies).
- Nadia Seferović: HN/47286820 ("ask your bank manager for rates on a 30 day deposit account … it appeared in my online banking the next day").
- Kevin Duarte: the launch post ("a mutual fund where your principal is at considerable risk – it had a 9% loss in 2022") and HN/47280944 (the short-term bond fund in "one of the leading startup treasury products"). Moving the loss to August 2026 is **[author]**.

Decision-makers (`link: COMMERCIAL_B2B`, `founder`, Part 3 only, no story on screen):
- Sofia Marchetti: author's invention, filling a gap: the thread has almost no willing buyer. She stands for the founders' own case ("putting $5M into Palus yields them an extra $50k-75k per year", HN/47290584) and the batchmates who "wanted this too" (HN). Her $2,000 a month is the bank's treasury fee.
- Jamal Booker: HN/47297953 ("That 50-75k is more like $5k/month out of what is typically a ~200-400k monthly burn") and HN/47401784 ("it definitely takes weeks to diligence").
- Eleanor Vance: HN/47279349 ("bet the company"); the board having to agree is **[author]**.
- Ravi Menon: HN/47279377 ("I am not sure I would suggest my portfolio companies to risk their treasuries"). The investor who had to agree is his.
- Maya Feldman: HN/47283895 (signed up) and HN/47283356 (liked "a number that goes up").
- Daniel Osei: HN/47283590 ("The probability is Low but the impact for us is massive"). The tax adviser's long sign-off is his.
- Irene Kowal: HN/47279831 ("This should be a hard pass for literally everyone … SGOV") and HN/47279261 ("just put the money in a Bond ETF").
- Felix Brandt: HN/47282750 ("I am willing to take a little bit more risk for a higher return … an extra month or two of runway").

No respondent carries a commenter's handle or a real customer's name (SITE names client companies; none is used).

## Open

- **Relative advantage code.** The registry fixes five advantage codes (fewer_attempts, shorter_time, less_worry, less_help_needed, easier_recovery). None means "more money". I used `less_help_needed` with the founder's label "Higher yield without hiring for treasury". It is the closest code, and it carries the founder's claim of "no need to hire for treasury operations" (HN/47283812). A yield code would fit better.
- **Price period.** Palus prices a share of the balance, not an amount per period. The $800 to $1,200 a month depends on the $4M to $6M reserve I chose. Keel has no "percent of balance" price.
- **Cost estimate kind.** The founder's cost is yield given up, not money spent. Decision-makers asked "what it cost the team last month" will report fees and hours, so Existing sacrifice is likely to read far below the founder's estimate. That is a real finding about this idea, but it is also partly an artefact of the question's wording.
- **Window.** The {3, MONTHS} window and the "cash decision" occasion are mine. Public material has no single trigger moment, only "drawn down gradually".
- **Not checked against the engine.** The file passes keel-e2e-eval's `instructions/corpus.py` loader (bound to the registry) and every rule of `sim/check_corpus_r12.py` but S/C/V. Those three need the `expected` block, which a back-test omits by design.

screens.why5: It keeps the founder's circumstance word for word, and nothing about a product or yield pitch reaches me.
screens.why6: Short, one question, "Yes or no" at the end; easy to answer on one hearing.
screens.instead: In the last 3 months, did you decide where your raise money is kept, including choosing to leave it where it was? Yes / No

screens.why1: A frequency question after the yes is the natural next step, but deciding where raise cash sits is something I did once after we closed and then left alone, so counting months is a bit of an odd thing to ask next.
screens.why2: 'On how many of those 3 months' is clumsy; I had to read it twice to see it means 'in how many of the last three months'.
screens.why3: I know when I moved the money, but whether a quick check of our Mercury balances or the treasury yield counts as 'deciding' in a given month is a guess.
screens.why4: The 0 contradicts the yes I just gave, so it is an odd option; 1, 2 and 3 cover it, and 'I can't recall' fits.
screens.why5: It is still about where the raise cash sits, in the founder's own words, and nothing about a product reaches me.
screens.why6: The question is short and said once, and 'zero, one, two, or three' is an easy list to hold.
screens.instead: Since the raise, how often have you changed where that cash sits? Once, when we set it up; two or three times; every month or so; or I can't recall.

screens.why1: Having just said I decided where the raise cash sits, asking what I'd most like made easier about that decision follows naturally.
screens.why2: "Your last cash decision" is looser than the earlier "where cash from a raise would sit" and could read as any spend or payment decision, though the options themselves are in my trade's words (insured limit, idle cash, runway).
screens.why3: I make exactly these calls on our Mercury accounts, so I can answer from what I actually do.
screens.why4: My real answer, keeping the setup simple with fewer accounts and platforms to run, is only partly covered by "moving money without mistakes", and "knowing the months of runway left" is a forecasting job more than a where-the-cash-sits one.
screens.why5: It stays on the founder's job of keeping raise cash safe and earning, with no product or plan showing through.
screens.why6: One short question with five short parallel options and a single escape said last, easy to hold on one hearing.
screens.instead: Think of the last time you decided where the raise cash would sit. Which two would you most like made easier? Getting cash back fast when needed; Keeping cash safe above the insured limit; Checking idle cash is earning enough; Keeping it simple with fewer accounts to run; or Moving money between accounts without mistakes. Or say None of these.

screens.why1: A follow-up on why I ranked things the way I did fits after the pick-two, but it arrives without saying which difficulty I passed over, so it feels abrupt.
screens.why2: "This one" never says which difficulty it means, so I'd have to scroll back and guess which of the options I didn't pick it's asking about.
screens.why3: Once I know which one it means, I can say why, from how I actually run our cash (for me the operational burden of moving money beats chasing yield).
screens.why4: A box to type in, no options.
screens.why5: Nothing of a product or the founder's own terms reaches me; it only asks about my own ranking.
screens.why6: Short and one question, but heard once, "this one" points at nothing I can hold, since the list was read a screen ago and the difficulty isn't named.
screens.instead: You didn't pick [the difficulty by name] as one to make easier. What made the other two more pressing for you?

screens.why1: After asking where I put the raise cash and what I'd want easier, asking how my current setup works is the obvious next step.
screens.why2: The stem is plain, but each option bundles rate and effort together, and 'upkeep' isn't how I'd describe managing a sweep or treasury account, so I'd have to reread to find mine.
screens.why3: I know exactly what we earn, about 3.2%, and how much work it takes, so I can answer from my own books.
screens.why4: My true answer, a fair rate with almost no effort, falls between 'good rate, no effort' and 'fair rate, a little upkeep'; 'low rate, never revisited' and 'little after fees and effort' overlap; and 'Someone else did it' is an odd escape for the person who runs the cash.
screens.why5: The job was keeping raise cash safe and earning, but the screen asks only about return and drops safety, which matters more to me than yield; nothing of the product leaks.
screens.why6: The stem and the five options say well, but each option carries two ideas split by a comma, so they are hard to hold by ear and compare on one hearing.
screens.instead: How well did the way you hold the company's spare cash work, on safety, rate and effort? Did what we needed with little effort; Fine but the rate could be better; Safe but takes too much of my time; Worried about safety above the insured limit; or We haven't really set it up. Or say I can't tell.

screens.why1: Right after I said our way of earning a return on spare cash works, asking what keeps it working is the obvious next thing to ask.
screens.why2: Plain to me, though "today's way" is a little vague; I'd read it as how we park the cash, which is what screen 6 was about.
screens.why3: I can answer from what I do: we keep it in Mercury's treasury sweep at about 3.2% because nobody has to touch it, and the low operational burden matters more to us than yield.
screens.why4: A box to type in, no options shown.
screens.why5: Screen 6 asked about earning a return, but this slides to "works for you", which could mean safety, access or low effort, so it drifts a little from earning and keeping the money safe; nothing of a product leaks.
screens.why6: Short, one question, nothing only the eye reads; it says well once.
screens.instead: You said the way you earn a return on the company's spare cash works. What do you do to keep it working?
